]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:31:49 +0000https://rdfandsparql.com/rdf12-sparq12-cheat-sheetMKolchinhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249649https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249649<![CDATA[Show HN: Flowfile – Open-source visual ETL that round-trips to Python (Polars)]]>Hi HN, I'm Edward, the author of Flowfile.

Flowfile is a visual ETL tool built on Polars. You build pipelines on a canvas, and every flow is also Python code. You can export it or write code with the FlowFrame API (Polars-like) and it shows up as a visual graph (or vice versa - keep reading).

Flowfile is what it is today because I believe we are spending too much time translating non-technical and technical implementations of data problems. Sometimes visual works better, and sometimes code. You should be able to choose whichever is easiest, without fully committing to one way of working. Flowfile solves this by standardizing the backend component without favoring either visual or code.

Which brings me to Flowfile's newest feature: notebook mode. The flow opens as Python cells that stay in sync with the canvas. If you add a filter (df.filter(...)) in a cell, it appears on the canvas. And it also works the other way around: if you add a sort on the canvas, it appears as a .sort(...) in the notebook. So now you can switch between visual and code without making a total mess of it under the hood.

It also has a data catalog, a scheduler, sandboxed Python execution, etc.. It's MIT licensed, and `pip install flowfile` installs all dependencies.

Github: https://github.com/edwardvaneechoud/Flowfile

I'd love feedback, especially on the notebook mode.

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:51:54 +0000https://github.com/KonradJuenger/ShowMecon____radhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249033https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249033<![CDATA[Show HN: Termcraft – 2D terminal survival with multiplayer support]]>Earlier this year, I started developing Termcraft, a terminal-based 2D survival game written in Rust.

Since its first release more than half a year ago, I've added multiplayer support, so you can now host a game and play with friends (or colleagues during a meeting?); Up to 8 players. I've also substantially improved the visuals, lighting, physics, and overall gameplay. A friend and I ended up spending the entire weekend playing through the game from start to finish.

The progression takes you from gathering wood and building a shelter to crafting equipment, exploring caves, finding diamonds, crossing the Nether, and fighting the Ender Dragon. There are villages, farming, collaborative building, PvP, and player chat along the way.

It's open source under the AGPL-3.0 license, with downloadable builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Gameplay demo video: https://youtu.be/nn37_15dLFM Installation and controls: https://pagel-s.github.io/termcraft/

It's not perfect, but I'd love to hear your feedback and experiences with the game. Contributions are also more than welcome!
